interviewQuestions.question: Why does using a `<div onclick>` instead of a `<button>` actually break accessibility, rather than just being a style preference?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It's a functional gap, not an aesthetic one, and the mechanism is worth explaining precisely: assistive technology like a screen reader doesn't read the DOM or CSS directly — it queries the **accessibility tree**, a separate structure the browser computes from your markup's semantic meaning, exposed through the operating system's accessibility API.

A `<button>` populates that tree correctly and automatically: the `button` role, keyboard focusability in the natural tab order, activation on both Enter and Space, and disabled-state handling, all for free. A `<div onclick>` contributes **nothing** to that tree by default — no role, no focusability — no matter how convincingly it's styled to look like a button on screen. A screen reader user hears it as plain text; a keyboard-only user can't Tab to it at all.

Reproducing the button's behavior manually means adding `role="button"`, `tabindex="0"`, a keydown handler for both Enter and Space (they're handled slightly differently by some browsers, which is a common source of a "works with Enter, not Space" bug), and manual disabled-state handling — real work that a native element gives you correctly and for free.

**Testing:** whether you can explain the actual mechanism (the accessibility tree) rather than just repeating "use semantic HTML" as a rule without understanding why it works.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through fixing a component built entirely from divs — no semantic elements, no landmarks, no real interactive elements — into an accessible one.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd work through it layer by layer rather than trying to fix everything in one pass, since the different problems have different fixes.

First, structure: replace layout-only divs that represent real page regions with the right landmark elements — `<nav>` for a navigation block, `<main>` for the primary content, `<header>`/`<footer>` where they genuinely apply — so a screen reader user gets the jump-between-landmarks shortcut instead of having to read the whole page linearly. Second, headings: confirm there's exactly one `<h1>` and that the rest form a real hierarchy without skipped levels, restyling with CSS rather than picking a heading level for its font size. Third, and usually the most common single fix: any `<div onclick>` masquerading as a button or link gets replaced with the actual `<button>` or `<a href>` — free keyboard focusability, free role, free activation behavior, and I remove whatever manual keydown/tabindex code was compensating for the wrong element choice.

After that pass, I'd do the actual test that catches what's left: unplug the mouse, Tab through the whole component, and confirm everything reachable that should be clickable actually is, in a sensible order, with a visible focus ring at every stop.

**Testing:** whether you have a systematic process for this rather than randomly sprinkling ARIA attributes until an automated scanner goes quiet.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Applied

interviewQuestions.question: When is it acceptable to use a generic element plus ARIA instead of a native semantic element, and when is that a mistake?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It's acceptable, and often necessary, when there's genuinely no native element for the interaction pattern — there's no `<tabs>` element, no `<combobox>` element with the exact behavior a design calls for, so a `<div>` with `role="tablist"`/`role="tab"` plus manually-managed keyboard behavior is the correct approach there, because the alternative is not building the widget at all.

It's a mistake when a native element already covers the exact case and gets skipped anyway — `role="button"` on a div when `<button>` would have done the same job with less code and zero risk of the ARIA attribute drifting out of sync with the actual element state. That drift is the real cost of the ARIA-instead-of-native route: a native `<button disabled>` can't lie about its own disabled state, but a div with `aria-disabled="true"` set once and never updated as the underlying state changes absolutely can, and does, in real codebases.

The rule I actually use: check for a native element first; reach for ARIA only for the genuine gaps HTML doesn't cover; and where ARIA is unavoidable, treat keeping its state attributes in sync with the actual UI as a first-class part of the component's logic, not an afterthought.

**Testing:** whether you understand ARIA as a fallback for genuine gaps, not a general substitute for the right element.
